e53bbe063a7ba2ff9e9a592a639bf7cf.text: Berta, a five-year-old Maremma livestock guardian dog, was discovered dead in a baited snare near her home west of Williams Lake. “If I would have known the dangers in my backyard, maybe she would have been able to be saved,” is the thought that keeps coming back to Victoria Savile of Williams Lake as she calls for change after her family’s beloved dog, Berta, was killed in a baited snare not far from their home. Savile has recently joined The Fur-Bearers, a Canadian wildlife protection charity dedicated to protecting fur-bearing animals through conservation, advocacy, research and education. She’s also working with Nicole Trigg whose dog, Moon, was killed by a baited trap off a public service road in the East Kootenays earlier this year. Berta died after becoming entangled in the trap Savile said was set not far from their property in the Pablo Creek area west of Williams Lake, in an area she has ridden her horses, hiked and hunted for the past eight years. Savile had never seen a snare, bait or been told a trapping line was present until Berta’s body was discovered on Sunday, Oct. 18 by a neighbour out quadding. In shock and overcome with emotion that morning, Savile called the RAPP (Report All Poachers and Polluters) line and in less than an hour conservation officers arrived to remove the trap from Berta, who had failed to return home earlier this month. She said officers helped load Berta’s body into her and her family’s truck, which they brought back home to bury in their backyard. Berta was a five-year-old Maremma livestock guardian dog adopted in Alberta who Savile described as a great protector in keeping predators away and everyone safe, including their neighbour’s sheep and goats. Her family loved calling her ‘Dirty Bert’ due to the fact her pure white coat was always stained by dirt that no one knew where from. “She was an absolute sweetheart and her life was taken from us,” Savile said. fbe7446fb20855b6af3b469b8a555cdf.text: Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor is presented with the first poppy this year by Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 First Vice President Al Tranq. The Royal Canadian Legion's National Poppy Campaign runs from Oct. 24 to Nov. 11. Poppies will be available in Williams Lake starting Friday, Oct. 23 as the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 distributes poppy boxes to local businesses in advance of Remembrance Day. The first poppy was presented earlier this week to Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor by Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 First Vice President Al Tranq at the cenotaph located outside city hall where flags were flying at half-mast in recognition of the tragic deaths at the Canadian Forces Base (CFB) in Wainwright. “Each year, Canadians step up with amazing support for the National Poppy Campaign,” stated Royal Canadian Legion Dominion President Sharon McKeown in a news release. “Their generosity and caring are what allow us to host a range of programs and support initiatives for our Veterans and their families across the country.” Poppies will be available right up until Nov. 11 where in Williams Lake there will be an indoor ceremony at the Cariboo Memorial Recreation Complex starting 10 a.m. in the Gibraltar Room. Doors open at 9 a.m. The Colour Party and those marching will then head over to the cenotaph outside city hall for a moment of silence and a wreath-laying ceremony. They’ll then march to the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 located at 385 Barnard St. to lay a wreath after which everyone is invited into the branch for food and camaraderie. A wreath or cross for the cenotaph display can still be rented by emailing poppy139@gmail.com or calling 250-305-7999.

The Vancouver-Quilchena riding, deep within a leafy-green, wealthy Vancouver neighbourhood, has long been a bastion of B.C.’s right wing. Former B.C. Liberal leaders Kevin Falcon, Andrew Wilkinson and Gordon Campbell all represented the riding for a spell. More recently, OneBC Leader Dallas Brodie, elected as a B.C. Conservative before she was ejected from the party, has held the seat. But with her running as a far-right alternative, and Carson Binda of the Canadian Taxpayers’ Federation running for the B.C. Conservatives, NDP candidate Callista Ryan suddenly sees an opening. “We’re pretty confident with the base that we have,” she said. “But we also do anticipate a vote split between Dallas Brodie and Carson Binda.” NDP Leader David Eby even stopped in the riding to help out on Thursday, with just two days to go before the election and his time more valuable than ever on the campaign trail. Mario Canseco of Research Co. points out that if Ryan gets the same vote she did in the riding in 2024, a bit more than 38 per cent, and Brodie manages 10 to 12 per cent, Binda and the Conservatives could lose what is otherwise a safe seat. Brodie, meanwhile, positions herself as the only true conservative candidate running in the riding. She is best known for her controversial stances on Indigenous rights. She argues that First Nations have unfairly capitalized on progress toward reconciliation to gain financially, and that property rights are in danger because of gains in Indigenous sovereignty. NDP Leader David Eby and OneBC Leader Dallas Brodie. On the eve of election day, B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is still explaining why he dissolved the legislature and called the snap vote when his party still had two years left on its mandate. “People are very surprised and frustrated by the election call,” he told reporters in Surrey on Friday. “I should have done a better job of letting them know how stalled out the legislature was.” His opponents have capitalized, with leaders of both the Conservative and Green parties calling it a “cynical” power grab. Eby called it his “biggest regret” of the campaign that he didn’t do a better job of filling voters in and convincing them it is needed for his party to govern effectively. Since the 2024 election, Eby’s party has shuffled along with a one-vote majority and often struggled to muster the votes to pass difficult legislation, such as amendments to the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act. In a sit-down interview on his campaign bus as he veered between key Lower Mainland ridings on the final day before election day, he explained the difficulties he says his government faced. “Even things as simple as allowing pets in rentals had to be sacrificed to be able to get other pieces through,” he said, referring to a 2024 election promise to mandate landlords allow pets in purpose-built rental buildings. He also mentioned Xavier’s Law, a private member’s bill introduced by NDP MLA Dana Lajeunesse following the death of 12-year-old Xavier Rasul-Jankovics, who was hit by a car and killed on Vancouver Island in 2025. 59f61017c339b9e4fa7288bea8865319.text: NDP leader David Eby (right) visited downtown Langley City with local candidates Holly Isaac (left) and Andrew Mercier (centre). NDP leader David Eby (right) visited downtown Langley City with local candidates Holly Isaac (left) and Andrew Mercier (centre). NDP leader David Eby said the 300-bed long-term care facility his government promised Langley before the last election would be built if he’s re-elected. Eby met with Langley-Willowbrook NPD candidate Andrew Mercier and Langley-Walnut Grove’s hopeful Holly Isaac on Friday, Oct. 23, in Langley City, visiting several local stores and chatting with people on the street in the final hours before the provincial election. Asked about the promised local facility, which was to be built on the grounds of Langley Memorial Hospital, Eby said there had been challenges in bringing down the per-bed cost of that planned facility and a number of others. The province was working to drive down the cost via standardization, he said. “Shovels will be in the ground on this and seven other long-term care facilities,” Eby said. He also acknowledged the need for more hospital services in the fast growing South of the Fraser region. “We need more health-care professionals and health-care services,” Eby said, arguing that the NDP’s plan would be fully funded, while alleging that the B.C. Conservatives would cut health services. The Conservatives have promised to protect health-care funding, recruit more doctors and nurses, and cut wait times. On another local issue, Mercier said that the NDP is promising a second Urgent Primary Care facility for Langley. The first local UPC opened in May 2024. They’re intended to take some pressure off overburdened hospital emergency rooms. Eby said that the funding for a new UPC could also be applied to a community health centre, a model in which towns and cities can have their own building with similar services and some municipal control. With 10 ridings up for grabs, including at least seven potential swing districts, both the NDP and Conservative leaders hit the campaign trail in Surrey in the days leading up to B.C. election day. B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson held a raucous rally in the Surrey-Newton riding in front of hundreds of fired-up supporters. Several local political heavyweights attended, including newly elected mayor Doug McCallum and former mayors Linda Hepner and Dianne Watts. Former premier Christy Clark was also there. “Everywhere we have been, it has been unbelievable,” Doerkson said, firing up the throng that surrounded and dwarfed him on a stage set up in the centre of a warehouse. “The absolute best crowds we’ve ever had.” Many experts believe control of the government will come down to how Surrey votes. In 2024, it was the same. The NDP’s Garry Begg won the pivotal Surrey-Guildford riding by just 22 votes, giving his party a one-seat majority in the legislature. Eby acknowledged the area’s importance during a Friday-morning campaign stop, pointing out that Surrey is on the path to becoming B.C.’s largest city and calling it the “economic engine” of the province. “All the promise is there, but so are all of the challenges,” he said. “When you’re fast growing, infrastructure gets strained. Health care gets strained, schools get strained.” Several attendees at Doerkson’s rally said health care is their number one issue. And his pledge to build a new women’s and children’s hospital got one of the biggest rounds of applause of the night. Supporter Harveer Grewal complained about the wait times for care at the Surrey Memorial Hospital. “If you’re waiting 10 to 14 hours for a doctor, how is that OK?” he asked. While promoting new drama series Yaga, filmed in and around Victoria, Heated Rivalry actor Hudson Williams offered a less-than-favourable review of B.C.’s capital when asked to name the city’s “hot spots.” “A lot of hot spots of, like, old people on their little scooters, people retiring,” he told Etalk. “Like, it’s Victoria. Hotspots for, like, what? Like retirement homes and fricking bingo, like that’s it. It’s not the first time the actor has taken a playful jab at Victoria’s reputation. While Williams’ words appear to be tongue-in-cheek, UVic isn’t letting the jabs go unanswered. The university has fired back at the actor with a playful social media post that pokes fun at his review while highlighting some of Greater Victoria’s attractions. 092f76289e140047d724462021b890f7.text: After the posted asphalt resurfacing project was actually seal coating, upset residents are frustrated with the large, loose rocks and jagged surface that are damaging vehicles. Jeff Seabrook shows the size of the rocks that now cover Chase-Falkland Road as a result of resurfacing work recently completed by the province. “This new road is supposed to be an upgrade, and it’s the exact opposite.” Jeff Seabrook, a resident of Chase-Falkland Road that was supposed to have asphalt resurfacing, said they’re literally getting dinged by the “bait and switch” project, and their vehicles are paying the price. According to a June 9 media release from the Ministry of Transportation and Transit (MoTT), more than $136 million was invested this year to resurface interior highways and local roads to ensure “drivers continue to have a safe and comfortable driving experience.” The project included 28.7 kilometres of Chase-Falkland. 6f6f5a70220bfb22658046536855d2f2.text: Quesnel RCMP are asking for witnesses and dashcam footage following a fatal pedestrian hit-and-run near Yellow Marker earlier this month. According to an RCMP press release, the incident occurred shortly before 3 a.m. on Oct. 5, when officers were called to Highway 97 south after a report of a man sitting on the side of the road. Mounties said the man was located and taken to the hospital with what initially appeared to be minor injuries. According to police, the man later died in the hospital from injuries sustained in what was determined to be a hit-and-run incident. Following an investigation, police determined the man had been struck by a red 2023 Volvo tractor-trailer. Mounties have since located the vehicle and identified its driver. “Our thoughts are with the family and friends of the victim during this distressing time,” Cpl. Jennifer Cooper, BC RCMP spokesperson for Northern B.C., said in the release. “What police officers are requesting is for any witnesses or anyone with dash camera footage that captures the incident to please come forward and provide their information.” Mounties said investigators are particularly seeking footage from vehicles travelling along Highway 97 south near Yellow Market between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m. on Oct. 5. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson at a rally in Surrey on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Lorne Doerkson has been sent back to Victoria for the third time by the voters of the Cariboo-Chilcotin, this time as premier of the entire province. Based on preliminary polls Doerkson, the incumbent MLA for the Conservative Party of B.C., has won 76.9 per cent of the vote as of 10:30 p.m., with 75 of 89 ballot boxes counted. His rivals, Kathryn Askew of the BC NDP, secured roughly 17.1 per cent of the vote, while Douglas Gook of the Green Party of B.C. brought home six per cent of the vote. As of Saturday, Oct. 24 at 9 p.m., the Conservative Party of B.C. is on track to form a majority government. This means that, if Doerkson’s interim-leader status is formalized, he will be B.C.’s next premier. Projections currently predict a 64-seat majority government for the Conservatives, with the NDP set to form the opposition with 27 seats. Speaking to a crowd of supporters Saturday night in Victoria, Doerkson was visibly excited and emotional. In his speech, he praised the volunteers who made this victory possible, both provincially and here in the Cariboo-Chilcotin. “To our volunteers, you knocked on doors, rain and shine, you did so much incredible work. You put up signs, you made the calls, none of this would have been possible without your hard work,” Doerkson said. “To everyone who voted tonight, including those who voted for someone else, thank you so very much. “I also want to thank my team at home, because they have done an unbelievable job. I will say this, Cariboo-Chilcotin is amazing!” During his speech, Doerkson mentioned the Cariboo several times when outlining his vision for B.C.’s future. 1a2abfe921b2de6235b0b7bf6f6b14ac.text: Doerkson set to become B.C. premier after projected Conservative majority win | Williams Lake Tribune Doerkson set to become B.C. premier after projected Conservative majority win Lorne Doerkson takes the stage as the B.C. Conservatives are the projected 2026 election winners by majority. Lorne Doerkson is poised to become British Columbia’s next premier after leading the Conservative Party to a projected majority government Saturday, Oct. 24, barely five weeks after taking over a party struggling with internal divisions. A projected Conservative majority was solidified shortly after 9 p.m., prompting loud cheers and sustained applause from supporters gathered at the party’s election-night headquarters at Rocky Mountaineer Station in Vancouver. An estimated 500 to 600 people attended the gathering, where supporters repeatedly erupted in applause as election results appeared on screens throughout the evening. Doerkson, 58, assumed the party’s interim leadership Sept. 20 following Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s resignation. Two days later, NDP Premier David Eby called a snap provincial election, sending British Columbians to the polls two years ahead of schedule. Doerkson is also being sent back to Victoria for the third time by the voters of the Cariboo Chilcotin. The Conservatives established leads across much of the province on Saturday, including several Metro Vancouver ridings previously held by the NDP. Doerkson was first elected to the legislature in 2020 as a BC Liberal, representing Cariboo-Chilcotin, and joined the Conservatives in 2024. Before entering provincial politics, he worked as a community newspaper publisher. His appointment as interim leader followed months of Conservative infighting, caucus departures and changes in party leadership. Following his appointment, several MLAs who had left or been expelled returned to the Conservative caucus. 150448b73a0f1e2ebf11526ab858bb91.text: B.C. Votes 2026: BC Conservative Pavneet Singh wins Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream riding | Williams Lake Tribune B.C. Votes 2026: BC Conservative Pavneet Singh wins Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream riding BC Conservative candidate Pavneet Singh arrives at the Fairfield Inn in Kelowna after winning the riding on final voting day, Oct. 24, 2026. BC Conservative candidate Pavneet Singh arrives at the Fairfield Inn in Kelowna after winning the riding on final voting day, Oct. 24, 2026. Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream has a new MLA, as the BC Conservatives’ Pavneet Singh has been elected. Singh beat out BC NDP candidate Binny Boparai, Green candidate Carter Mochinski and OneBC candidate Alexandra Wright to win the riding. In a brief interview with media, Singh thanked volunteers and supporters. Media, including Black Press, were barred by the Conservative campaign managers on scene from listening to Singh’s victory speech at the Fairfield Inn on Powick Road on election night on Oct. 24. Singh told media, “Today is not the time for media interviews, today is for the volunteers, family and friends who supported us.” Singh said he would be available for interview at a later date. With one ballot box left to be counted, Singh has 47.44 per cent of the vote (10,453 votes).

With a Conservative Party of BC majority government forecast, and with Conservative candidate Megan Knight projected to win the riding of Surrey South, CentreBC leader and Surrey South candidate Elenore Sturko was a little emotional as she spoke to her team at CentreBC headquarters Saturday night. The CentreBC office was filed with positive energy throughout election night, despite the party not being projected to win any seats in the provincial legislature. “I’m a bit emotional as I deliver this speech tonight, but please know it’s not because I’m sad. It’s because I’ve so enjoyed serving my community and the gravity of knowing how many of you supported me during these last four years of elected service, and now that that is changing, it’s heavy,” Sturko told her supporters, other CenterBC candidates, and volunteers after former NDP premier David Eby conceded the majority Conservative win. “Tonight the results may not be what we hoped for. We may not have won a seat in the legislature and I know it’s disappointing because we did work hard. We believed in what we were building and we wanted the opportunity to put our ideas into action. But I want you to remember something,” Sturko continued. “The value of what we have accomplished cannot be measured by the number of seats that we’ve won tonight. Just weeks ago Center BC was a party with potential but limited resources, a small team, and a long work ahead of us. Together we built something very special. We recruited candidates across British Columbia. We brought new voices into public life, developed great platforms focused on practical solutions, and took our message directly to the people,” she said. Provincewide, Conservatives lead in 63 ridings, compared with 28 for the NDP and two for the Greens. Polls have closed across B.C., and counting has started except in Grassy Plains, on the Southside of Francois Lake in the Nechako Lakes riding of Northwest B.C., where the polling station will remain open until 10 p.m. Elections B.C. confirmed that voters on the Southside would have the extra two hours tonight after the polls opened late this morning, after 10 a.m. Today, Oct. 24, is the final day to vote in the provincial election. British Columbians are heading to the polls to vote for MLAs in 93 ridings across the province. Polls opened at 8 a.m. and will close at 8 p.m., local time. A live blog will be updated throughout the evening with coverage from party headquarters. NDP Leader David Eby called the snap election on Sept. 22 after about a week of speculation as the B.C. Conservative Party dissolved into chaos, and Kerry-Lynne Findlay quit as party leader. Two days before the election call, Lorne Doerkson was named interim Conservative leader, unifying the party and bringing more than a dozen MLAs who had quit under Findlay back into the fold before the election was called. Amid a steady chorus of boos, Quinn Hughes had a goal and an assist, lifting the visiting Minnesota Wild to a 4-2 win over the Vancouver Canucks in NHL action Sunday at Rogers Arena in Vancouver. Hughes, the superstar defenceman and former Canucks captain, was returning to Vancouver for the first time since being acquired by Minnesota on Dec. 12, 2025. He was loudly jeered every time he touched the puck, along with various derogatory chants during the game. A tribute video during a break seven minutes into the first period drew a mixture of cheers and boos, with Hughes acknowledging the fans with a raised stick. Maxim Shabanov, Bobby Brink and Kirill Kaprizov also scored for the Wild (8-3-2), with Calvin Pickard making 15 saves for the goaltending win. Max Sasson and Brock Boeser scored for the Canucks (2-10-1), who have dropped 10 straight games. Leevi Merilainen took the loss for Vancouver, stopping 30 of 34 shots. The Canucks came out strong, not allowing the Wild a shot for the first six minutes, but they could not beat Pickard. With 1:27 left in the period, Shabanov tapped in a no-look, cross-crease pass from Kaprizov for his third goal of the season, on a Wild power play. The Wild began to take control in the middle frame. Brink made it 2-0 at 5:54, making a slick move to fool Merilainen and scoring his first goal of the year. Seven minutes later on another Wild power play, Hughes scored his third of the year, slipping out from behind the net to knock in a rebound to the left of Merilainen. It was the 500th point of his NHL career. In the third period, Hughes sprung Kaprizov for a breakaway, and he beat Merilainen at 3:38 for his 13th of the year. 8037bcbc8635712289cdc7690574ea32.text: Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson addresses the media in Vancouver on Oct. 25, 2026, the morning after his sweeping electoral victory. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson pitched unity and quick action in his first media appearance just 12 hours after leading the B.C. Conservative Party to a sweeping electoral victory. “To the British Columbians who voted for another party yesterday, I heard you,” he said. “Starting today, I am your premier as much as anyone else’s. You will have a government that listens to you, works for you, and respects you, however you marked your ballot.” Because he was appointed to lead his party just two days before the Sept. 22 snap election call, Doerkson is technically the interim leader. But he brushed aside the notion that he would step aside and allow for a leadership race. “I am leader, and that’s an administrative detail,” he said. “There’ll be more information on that imminently, but I will remain as leader of the party, and I’m thrilled to be the premier of British Columbia right now.” He says he will act quickly to address emergency room closures that have plagued small communities throughout B.C., promising that within his first 100 days in office he will establish a commission to work on keeping ERs open and cutting wait times. As the MLA for the Cariboo-Chilcotin riding, Doerkson knows the concerns with recurring temporary closures of emergency services, with 100 Mile House’s ER having more than 37 closures this year. Doerkson was re-elected to a third term in the riding. He also promises an independent review of the government’s finances. B.C.’s deficit is nearly $14 billion, and multiple credit rating agencies downgraded the province’s rating in recent years. “Before we table a budget, you will have the full picture,” he said. Doerkson also says he will immediately work on promised changes to election rules to avoid overlapping provincial and municipal elections. 655c8bdab7ead0583824131a37668dd8.text: 2026 B.C. election sees record low turnout as Conservatives win majority | Williams Lake Tribune 2026 B.C. election sees record low turnout as Conservatives win majority A large number of British Columbians opted out of the democratic process in the 2026 provincial election, according to preliminary results. The elections, which resulted in a landslide victory for the BC Conservatives on Oct. 24, saw the lowest turnout in the province’s history, with only 48.1 per cent of registered voters casting their ballots with 99.75 per cent of boxes reporting. The result marks an over 10 per cent decrease in voter turnout percentage compared to the 2024 provincial elections, and is nearly six per cent lower than B.C.’s second-worst voter turnout in 2020, during the COVID pandemic. As of Sunday afternoon, Oct. 25, ElectionsBC had 1,798,103 votes considered of 3,738,182 registered voters, which represents the lowest number of total votes since the 2009 election. ElectionsBC is still counting vote-by-mail ballots, assisted telephone voting ballots, absentee ballots cast at special voting opportunities and absentee ballots cast on final voting day. BC NDP Leader David Eby, and now former premier, called the election two years early in an attempt to win a majority for the party’s fourth term. The snap election was announced about a week after the governing party’s main political opponents, the BC Conservatives, lost the former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay as she resigned. Since then, Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA Lorne Doerkson took the helm for the BC Conservatives on a technical interim basis. Speaking to reporters on Oct. 25, Doerkson said the interim label is an “administrative detail” and expects to be the leader of the party and the next Premier of B.C. NDP leader after party loses election Former premier David Eby is led off the stage by his wife Cailey Lynch after conceding the 2026 B.C. election. David Eby has conceded the 2026 B.C. election and stepped down as B.C. NDP leader. “This is obviously something I do with a heavy heart,” he told supporters gathered in downtown Vancouver on Saturday night. “But it is time for new leadership within our party.” Eby called the snap election on Sept. 22 as the opposition Conservative Party looked to be in disarray. Former Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findaly stepped down just two days earlier amid a caucus uprising, and the party appeared to be splitting in two. But Lorne Doerkson took the helm as interim Conservative leader, and quickly unified the ranks. He is now projected to be premier-designate after leading the party to a sweeping electoral victory. Eby is still projected to win the Vancouver-Point Grey riding, but the Conservative Party appears to have flipped nearly 20 seats. Bowinn Ma, the NDP’s candidate for North Vancouver-Lonsdale, thanked former NDP Leader David Eby for his service and backed him up for calling the snap election. “I understand why he called this election,” she said. “We were dealing with a very slim majority, which we made work, definitely, but we did so at the expense of many of our MLAs, who sacrificed their health.” Eby has said that with a one-vote majority, passing legislation was difficult. Langley-Walnut Grove Conservative incumbent celebrated with her family after her second provincial electoral win on Saturday. Langley-Willowbrook NDP candidate Andrew Mercier and Langley-Walnut Grove candidate Holly Isaac were at the NDP election night event. Incumbent Conservative MLA Misty Van Popta held her riding again, and will now be heading to Victoria as part of the governing party. With all the election day ballots reporting and three of four advance ballot boxes counted, Van Popta was ahead with 7,552 votes, or 55.44 per cent of the total cast. Holly Isaac of the NDP received 4,362 votes, or 32.02 per cent. Green Party’s Sam Meyer received 1,107 votes for 8.13 per cent, and Kyle Stevenson of CentreBC took 586 votes, or 4.3 per cent. The party’s local success came as the Conservatives won a majority government. “More than Langley has spoken for that decisive change,” said Van Popta. She said she was thankful for her support, and also thanked the other candidates who had run against her for putting their names forward. “You never look at the polls, the only thing that matters is today,” she said. Once in Victoria, Van Popta said her priorities would be Langley Memorial Hospital, long-term care, and schools. “I’m obviously disappointed we didn’t get the result were looking for,” Isaac said. She said she was proud of her campaign team and extended her congratulations to Van Popta. The new riding was first contested in 2024, after boundaries were re-drawn. From 2020 to 2024, much of that region was represented by Megan Dykeman of the NDP, who was unseated by Van Popta. Langley-Willowbrook NDP candidate Andrew Mercier and Langley-Walnut Grove candidate Holly Isaac were at the NDP election night event. B.C. Conservative incumbent Jody Toor held her position as MLA for Langley-Willowbrook on Saturday, as her party took enough seats to easily form a majority government. d85e7fd6b5e77ef2142078f7bb8d5eac.text: Macklin McCall was re-elected in the West Kelowna-Peachland riding in the 2026 provincial election. Macklin McCall has been re-elected in West Kelowna-Peachland in a landslide vote. With just two ballot boxes left to be counted, McCall has more than 62 per cent of the vote, according to the preliminary numbers. “What a humbling and exciting night, I am honoured to be re-elected as your MLA and grateful for the trust our community has placed in me once again,” McCall said in an emailed statement to Black Press Media. “This is an opportunity to get results on the priorities that matter most to residents, including healthcare, housing, infrastructure, and support for local businesses.” The BC Conservative Party has also won a majority government for the first time in nearly 100 years. “Tonight, British Columbians voted for change and chose a BC Conservative government focused on the issues that matter most: affordability, public safety, healthcare, and economic opportunity,” said McCall. In 2024, McCall won the riding with 50.9 per cent of the vote. Now, he’ll be returning to Victoria to represent West Kelowna-Peachland. “I look forward to returning to Victoria with a strong mandate to represent our community and deliver on the commitments we made during this campaign,” added McCall. “Tonight we celebrate. Tomorrow, the work begins… thank you, West Kelowna-Peachland. It is an honour to serve you.”
